title: The Head Nod & Its Dialects
hook: The smallest gesture men trade is a flick of the head, and whether it goes up or down, once or three times, changes what it means.
why:
The nod is the most frequent gesture most men make, and the least examined. It greets a neighbour across a street, keeps a friend talking, signals agreement in a meeting, hurries a speaker along, and, in some countries, means no. Because it is so small and so automatic, men rarely notice their own nodding, and rarely question what another man's nod means.

The chapter on cultural calibration in Part VI promised that this part would take nods apart in detail. This chapter does. It covers the nod as a greeting, up and down; the nod as the engine of conversation, which researchers call backchannel; what speed and repetition add; the surprising evidence that nodding changes the mind of the person doing it; the places where a nod does not mean yes; the meaning of a nod withheld; and how to use your own nods honestly. By the end you should hear nods as clearly as words.

teach.h: Up or down: the nod as a greeting.
teach.p:
Two men pass on a street, at a petrol station, across a gym. Neither stops. One gives the other a nod, and it is returned. In many English-speaking places, men distinguish two versions without ever being taught them. The up-nod, a quick lift of the chin, tends to be casual and familiar: I see you, we know each other or we are the same sort, no need to stop. The down-nod, a short dip of the head, tends to be more formal or respectful: I acknowledge you, good day, I mean no trouble.

This is a folk taxonomy rather than a research finding. The distinction is widely recognised, but it has not been carefully studied, and its meanings shift between regions, generations and groups. Among some men, the up-nod is reserved for friends and the down-nod for strangers; among others, it is the reverse. Treat any rule you hear about it as local knowledge, to be checked against the men around you.

What holds more generally is that the nod is the smallest rung on the greeting ladder described in the previous chapter. It acknowledges without committing. It can also be pointedly withheld: a man who usually nods to you and stops doing so is telling you something, and a man who nods to everyone in a group except you is telling you something louder.

When you receive a nod, return it in the same form if you can, as you would match a handshake. When you give one, notice which way your own head goes. The figure here lifts his chin a few degrees. From across a car park, that small movement can carry the whole of a relationship.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men used up-nods and down-nods interchangeably with no difference in meaning. The distinction is widely reported but not systematically studied, so its meaning in any place should be learned from the people there.

teach.p:
In 1970 the linguist Victor Yngve gave a name to the small signals a listener sends while someone else is talking: the nods, the mm-hms, the yeahs that do not claim a turn. He called them the back channel. Speakers depend on them more than they realise. A speaker who gets no back channel at all, from a listener who stays perfectly still, typically falters, repeats himself, or asks whether the listener is following.

The linguist Evelyn McClave, in a detailed study published in 2000, catalogued many functions of head movements in conversation: nods that signal understanding, that mark a speaker's own emphasis, that invite the listener to respond, that express uncertainty or include a group. Speakers often seem to seek a nod at the end of a phrase, and listeners' nods tend to fall into rhythm with the speaker's own head movements. Conversation is partly a dance of heads.

For a reader, this means nods are among the best guides to whether a conversation is working. A listener who nods at the right moments is following. A listener whose nods come at random, or a beat late, may be thinking about something else. A speaker who keeps pausing and looking at you is asking for back channel, and if you give none, he will start to doubt himself.

The figure here is at the bottom of a nod, chin dropped toward the chest. In a conversation, that movement, repeated at the right moments, is the listener's half of the work. Without it, the speaker is talking into a void.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if speakers carried on unaffected when listeners gave no back channel. Studies of conversation consistently find that they do not, though how much they depend on nods rather than sounds or facial expressions varies between people and settings.

teach.p:
Nods differ in speed, size and number, and the differences carry meaning. A single, slow nod, often with a slight pause before it, usually says I hear you, go on. Two or three slow nods can say I agree, or that makes sense. Rapid, repeated, small nods, especially while the speaker is still in the middle of a sentence, often say yes, yes, I have got it, which can mean move along or let me speak.

Timing adds more. A nod that comes just after the speaker's key point says that the point landed. A nod that comes before the point is finished can mean the listener already knows what is coming, or wants to get on. A nod that lags behind the conversation can mean the listener is processing something hard, or is not really listening.

These are common patterns rather than fixed meanings. Some men nod constantly as a habit, and their nods mean little more than I am awake; others rarely nod, and a single nod from them is worth a speech. Some neurodivergent people nod less, or differently, and a Part V chapter addresses this. As with everything in this book, read a man's nodding against his own baseline before deciding what it means.

The figure here listens, upright and attentive, at work. His nods in the next minute will tell the speaker whether to go on, explain more, or stop. If you are the speaker, watch for the change from slow nods to fast ones. It is often the clearest sign that you have said enough.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the speed and number of nods carried no reliable meaning. Conversation research supports the general pattern, but individual habits vary so much that meanings must be checked against the person's baseline.

teach.p:
In 1980 Gary Wells and Richard Petty asked students to test headphones while listening to a radio editorial. Some were told to move their heads up and down while listening, supposedly to check how well the headphones stayed on; others to shake their heads side to side; others to keep still. Those who had been nodding agreed more with the editorial than those who had been shaking their heads.

Later work by Pablo Briñol and Petty, published in 2003, suggested what was going on. Nodding seemed to increase people's confidence in whatever they were thinking at the time. When the argument they heard was strong, and their thoughts about it favourable, nodding made them more persuaded. When the argument was weak, and their thoughts critical, nodding made them more confident in their criticisms, and they were less persuaded.

There are two lessons here. The first is about you as a listener. If you nod along out of politeness in a meeting, you may be strengthening whatever you happen to be thinking, and you may also leave the speaker believing that you agree. Notice when you are nodding, and ask yourself whether you mean it.

The second is a caution. These studies changed the listener's own head movements; they did not show that making another person nod makes them agree. Advice that tells you to nod at people to make them say yes goes beyond the evidence, and in this book's terms it is manipulation. The figure here leans in, attentive. Let his nods follow his thinking, not lead it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if nodding had no effect on the nodder's own attitudes or confidence. The original study is decades old and the later work is a conceptual extension rather than a direct repetition, so treat the effect as plausible rather than settled.
teach.pullQuote: Let your nods follow your thinking, not lead it.

teach.h: Dialects: a nod is not always yes.
teach.p:
Head movements for yes and no are among the gestures people most assume are universal, and they are not. In Bulgaria the conventions are widely described as reversed: a movement that looks like a nod can mean no, and a sideways movement can mean yes, though many Bulgarians switch to the international pattern with visitors. In Greece, Cyprus, parts of Turkey and nearby regions, no is often signalled by a quick upward toss of the head, sometimes with raised eyebrows and a click of the tongue, a gesture that a visitor can easily mistake for a casual up-nod.

In much of South Asia, a side-to-side tilt or wobble of the head can mean yes, I understand, or all right, depending on the region and the moment. Visitors often read it as uncertainty or refusal.

And in some cultures, nods are more frequent and mean listening rather than agreement. In 1990 the linguist Senko Maynard compared conversations in Japanese and American English and found that Japanese listeners nodded and gave other back-channel responses more often. Those nods typically mean I am following, not I agree. The chapter on cultural variance in Part I described students nodding calmly and then being unable to do the exercise. The nod was attention, not understanding.

The figure here lifts his chin. In London it might be a greeting; in Athens it might be a refusal. Where you are matters more than the movement. When it counts, confirm in words.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if nods meant yes everywhere. Descriptions of national patterns are well established for some places but can exaggerate uniformity within a country, so learn the local pattern from people who live there.

teach.p:
Sometimes the most important nod is the one that does not come. In meetings, senior men sometimes give no back channel at all, sitting still and stone-faced while a junior colleague presents. It may be concentration, habit or a deliberate show of status, and for the speaker it is unnerving whichever it is. Among friends, a man who stops nodding while you talk may have stopped agreeing, or may be thinking about something you said a minute ago.

Before you read a missing nod as disapproval, consider the rivals. Some men simply nod very little. Some people concentrate with their whole body still. Some cultures value an impassive face while listening. Some neurodivergent people find nodding on cue effortful or unnatural. Someone on a video call may be nodding at a screen that shows them nothing. And a man who is upset by what you are saying may freeze altogether.

The useful move is to check, not to guess. A speaker can pause and ask, “Does that make sense so far?”, which gives the listener an easy way in. A friend can say, “You've gone quiet; what do you think?” If the absence of nods is a status display, a question asked calmly is also the best way to take the pressure off yourself.

The figure here sits with arms folded, listening. Folded arms and a still head can mean disagreement, cold, comfort or concentration. Only his baseline, and a question, can tell you which.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a listener who did not nod always disagreed. The rivals listed here are common, which is why a missing nod should prompt a question rather than a conclusion.

teach.p:
Once you hear nods, you can use your own better. As a listener, especially when a man is telling you something difficult, slow nods at the end of his phrases are among the most effective encouragements you can give. They say go on without interrupting, and they are especially useful side by side, as the opening chapter of this part described, where your face is not available.

Avoid fast nodding when someone is struggling to say something; it can feel like being hurried. Avoid nodding to agree with something you do not agree with. In meetings, the habit of nodding along leaves people believing they have your support, and the later discovery that they did not is worse than an honest question at the time.

In settings where nods may mean different things, confirm agreement in words. “So we're agreed on the delivery date?” costs nothing and prevents the kind of misunderstanding that can sink a deal or a friendship. When someone gives you an up-nod or a down-nod in greeting, return it in kind.

Finally, notice your own baseline. If you nod constantly, your nods carry little information, and people may stop trusting them. If you rarely nod, people may read you as cold or disapproving when you are simply listening. Either way, it is worth knowing. The figures here stand angled toward each other in conversation. Much of what passes between them in the next few minutes will be carried by the movement of two heads.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if listeners' nods made no difference to how freely a speaker talked. Conversation research suggests that back channel matters, though the best amount differs between people and cultures.

poseGallery.doCaption: Slow nods that say go on
poseGallery.annotation: A speaker with no back channel starts to doubt himself. Slow nods at the end of his phrases keep him going without interrupting.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Fast nods with an eye on the clock
poseGallery.annotation: Rapid nods while someone is mid-sentence often say hurry up. If you have the time, let your nods slow down with his words.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Taking a nod as a yes
poseGallery.annotation: In many settings a nod means I am listening, not I agree. When it matters, confirm the decision out loud.

poseGallery.doCaption: Slow nods, sitting back, letting her finish
poseGallery.dontCaption: Nodding fast, leaning in, waiting to speak
poseGallery.annotation: Fast nods mid-sentence can feel like being hurried. A slow nod at the end of a phrase says go on, and leaves room for the next pause.
Some people never nod. Check their baseline and the rest of the room, and ask in words when it matters.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking in words: is that a yes?
poseGallery.dontCaption: Taking an upward toss of the head as yes
poseGallery.annotation: Head movements for yes and no vary across cultures. When the answer matters, a quick question saves a costly misreading.

caseStudy:
Callum, thirty-six, leads a project for a manufacturer in Leeds. He flies to Osaka to agree a delivery schedule with a supplier. The meeting goes, he thinks, perfectly. As he presents the timetable, the three engineers across the table nod steadily, and the senior engineer nods slowly at each of the key dates. Callum reports to his director that the dates are agreed.

A week later an email arrives proposing different dates, politely but firmly. Callum is baffled and a little angry. His director, who has worked with Japanese partners for years, explains that the nods probably meant that the engineers were following, attentively and courteously, not that they had accepted anything. A Japanese colleague in Leeds confirms it, and adds that the senior engineer's silence after the presentation, which Callum had taken as satisfaction, probably meant there were concerns he did not want to raise in front of others.

On the next call, Callum changes his approach. After each key date he pauses and asks directly, “Is this date possible for your team?” He arranges a smaller follow-up call with the senior engineer alone. The concerns come out: a component shortage nobody had mentioned. They agree new dates, and this time Callum confirms each one in writing.

He also starts noticing his own nods. In his director's meetings he catches himself nodding along to ideas he thinks are wrong, and realises that his colleagues have probably been reading his nods the way he read the engineers'. He begins to save his nods for agreement, and to ask questions instead.
observe: Notice the nods men give each other in passing today, up or down, and who gives which to whom.
In your next conversation, notice when the other person nods, and whether their nods speed up or slow down.
Notice your own nodding in a meeting, and whether each nod means that you agree.
Notice a moment when someone stops nodding while you are talking, and consider the rival explanations before deciding what it means.

drills.name: Nod Count
steps: Watch a recorded interview or talk show for ten minutes with the sound on.
Count the listener's nods, and note whether each was slow, fast, single or repeated.
Note what the speaker was saying just before each nod.
Watch the same section with the sound off and see whether you can tell, from the nods alone, how the conversation was going.
Write down two patterns you noticed.
variations: Do the count for a different kind of programme, such as a political interview, and compare the listener's nods.
Count your own nods during a recorded call or meeting, if you can watch it back, and note what they followed.

drills.name: Back Channel Experiment
steps: With a willing friend who knows what you are doing, ask him to tell you about his week for three minutes.
For the first minute, give natural nods; for the second, give none and stay still; for the third, nod fast and often.
Ask him how each minute felt to him as the speaker.
Swap roles, so that you feel the difference too.
Write down what you learned about the effect of your nods.
variations: Try a third minute in which you give only fast nods, and ask your friend how that felt compared with slow ones.
Do the experiment on a video call, and compare how much the missing back channel affects the speaker on screen.

drills.name: Nod Audit
steps: In your next meeting, notice each time you nod.
After the meeting, note whether each nod meant agreement, understanding or simply politeness.
Identify one nod that may have given a false impression.
Decide what you will do instead next time, such as asking a question.
variations: Ask a colleague you trust whether they have ever read one of your nods as agreement when you did not mean it.
In your next meeting, replace one automatic nod with a short question, and notice the response.

drills.name: Local Dialect
steps: Choose a country or community you deal with, or one you will visit.
Find out how people there signal yes, no and I am listening with the head.
Ask someone from that place to show you and to check your understanding.
Write down the signals you might misread, and the phrase you will use to confirm agreement in words.
variations: Ask a colleague or friend from another culture which of your gestures they found confusing when they first met you.
Find a video of people speaking in the language of the place you chose, and watch how listeners use their heads.

quiz.q: A colleague says that a nod means yes in every culture, so it is the one gesture you can always trust. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; nodding for yes is one of the few universal gestures
It is wrong: in some places nods are reversed or mean only listening
He is right, though nods mean yes more strongly in some countries
Nods mean nothing anywhere, so they should be ignored in conversation
quiz.explain: Bulgarian conventions are widely described as reversed, an upward head toss means no in Greece and nearby regions, and frequent nods in some cultures signal attention rather than agreement. Confirm agreement in words when it matters.

quiz.q: What did Wells and Petty find when students moved their heads while listening to an editorial through headphones?
options: Students who were nodding agreed more with the editorial than those shaking
Head movements made no difference at all to what students believed
Students who shook their heads remembered more of what had been said
Students who kept still were the most persuaded by the editorial
quiz.explain: Nodding listeners agreed more than those who shook their heads. Later work suggests that nodding increases confidence in whatever a person is thinking at the time.

quiz.q: According to Briñol and Petty's later work, what happened when people nodded while hearing a weak argument?
options: They were more persuaded, because nodding always increases agreement
They forgot the argument, because nodding distracted their attention
They were less persuaded, because nodding boosted their own criticisms
They became angry, because nodding conflicted with their real views
quiz.explain: Nodding seemed to increase confidence in people's own thoughts. With a weak argument their thoughts were critical, so nodding made them more confident in their criticism and less persuaded.

quiz.q: A friend is telling you, haltingly, about a hard week. You want him to keep talking. What fits this chapter best?
options: Stay completely still, so that he does not feel watched or judged
Nod quickly and often, so that he knows you understand everything
Interrupt with your own similar story, so that he feels less alone
Give slow nods at the end of his phrases, and let the pauses stay
quiz.explain: Slow nods at natural pauses are a form of back channel that says go on without interrupting. Fast nods can feel like hurrying, and stillness can leave him unsure whether you are following.

quiz.q: Three engineers nod steadily throughout your presentation, in a country where nods often mean I am listening. What should you do before reporting agreement?
options: Report that they agreed, since they nodded at every key point
Ask directly whether each key date works, and confirm it in writing
Assume they disagreed, since nodding there usually means the opposite
Wait for them to raise objections, since they will if there are any
quiz.explain: Nods can signal attention rather than agreement, and objections may not be raised in front of others. Asking directly about each point, and confirming in writing, avoids a costly misunderstanding.

quiz.q: What did Victor Yngve mean by the back channel?
options: The private side conversations that happen during a group meeting
The signals of mistrust that leak out when someone is being deceptive
The formal channel through which complaints are made at work
A listener's small nods and sounds that do not claim a turn to speak
quiz.explain: Yngve used the term for the nods, mm-hms and other small signals listeners send without taking over the conversation. Speakers depend on them to know that they are being followed.

quiz.q: What did Evelyn McClave's detailed study of head movements in speech find?
options: Head movements serve many functions in speech, well beyond yes and no
Head movements have only one function, which is to signal agreement with the speaker
Head movements are random and carry no information for the people in a conversation
Head movements are used only by listeners and never by the people who are speaking
quiz.explain: McClave catalogued many functions of head movements in conversation, including marking emphasis, lists and the speaker's turn, as well as back channel. A nod is rarely just a yes.

quiz.q: You ask a Greek colleague, who is on the phone, whether a report will be ready tomorrow. He tilts his head back sharply, raises his eyebrows and clicks his tongue. What fits this chapter best?
options: Take it as a quick up-nod meaning yes, and plan around the report tomorrow
Assume he is annoyed at being interrupted and wait for him to raise it later
Check in words, once he is off the phone, whether that was a yes or a no
Take it as a sign that he has not understood and ask your manager instead
quiz.explain: In Greece and nearby regions, an upward toss of the head with raised eyebrows often means no. When an answer matters, check it in words rather than reading a gesture through your own dialect.

quiz.q: Someone says that if you nod while you talk, the people listening will start to agree with you. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since nodding is one of the most reliable persuasion techniques
Research found nodding mainly affects the nodder's confidence, and it is not a trick
It is right, but only if you nod at least three times at each important point
It is right for audiences of men but not for audiences that include women
quiz.explain: Wells and Petty, and Briñol and Petty, found effects on the people who nodded, not on the people watching. This book does not teach nodding as a way of steering others.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific conversation in the past week in which nods mattered: one where you nodded without meaning it, where someone's nod misled you, or where a nod was withheld. Describe what happened, what the nods or their absence seemed to mean at the time, and what you now think they meant. Then consider your own baseline: do you nod a lot or a little, and how might other people be reading your nods?
reflection.guidance: Nods are easy to overlook, so it helps to anchor your answer in a concrete moment and the specific movements: up or down, fast or slow, one or many. If you are unsure how you come across, ask someone who knows you well how much you nod and what they take it to mean.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat a nod as a yes: in a meeting, a negotiation or a conversation across cultures, nods often mean only that someone is listening. The second is to read a missing nod as disapproval without considering habit, concentration, culture, neurodivergence or a frozen screen. The third is to nod along when you do not agree, leaving people believing they have your support. The fourth is to hurry a struggling speaker with fast nods, or to leave him talking into silence with none. And the fifth is to treat nodding as a technique for making other people agree, which goes beyond the evidence and crosses into manipulation. Hear the nods, check what they mean, and keep your own honest.

moreCases.title: The interviewer who never nodded
moreCases.scene:
Aisha, twenty-nine, is presenting to a panel of three for a promotion to team leader. Two of the panel, Clare and Ravi, nod as she speaks,
  smile at her examples and make the small sounds of listeners who are following. The third, Mr Grant, the director, does not move. He sits back,
  his face still, his pen moving steadily across his notepad. He does not nod once in twenty minutes.

  Aisha finds herself presenting to him alone. Each time she reaches a key point, she glances at him for a sign and gets nothing. By the middle of
  the presentation she has started to speed up, repeat herself and add qualifications she had not planned. She skips her strongest example because
  she is sure he is unimpressed. Afterwards, in the corridor, she tells a friend that she has blown it.

  Two days later she gets the job. Clare tells her, laughing, that Mr Grant gave her the highest score on the panel, and that he never nods at
  anyone.

Aisha had prepared for weeks. She had practised the presentation in front of her partner, who nodded encouragingly throughout, and she had come to depend on that rhythm without realising it. In the interview room, one face without it was enough to unsettle her.

Clare had noticed Aisha faltering and tried to help, nodding more and smiling more, which only made the contrast with Mr Grant starker. She told Aisha afterwards that she had wanted to say, "He's always like that," but could not, in the middle of an interview.
moreCases.misread:
Aisha read Mr Grant's missing back channel as disapproval, because a listener who gives no nods usually seems unconvinced. She then changed her presentation to win a reaction that was never going to come.

And because she was watching the still face, she stopped watching the two faces that were nodding, which were telling her exactly what she needed to know.

She also read the panel as a single audience, when it was three people with three different styles, two of them telling her clearly that she was doing well.

Mr Grant, for his part, had no idea of the effect he was having. He had sat on dozens of panels and had never been told.
moreCases.betterRead:
Yngve's back channel, the nods and small sounds that tell a speaker to go on, matters so much that a speaker who gets none typically falters, as Aisha did. But a missing nod has many causes besides disapproval: concentration, habit, note-taking, culture, neurodivergence or a deliberate effort to stay neutral on an interview panel. Mr Grant's steady note-taking was a sign of attention, not rejection. The better reading starts with the rivals and with the people who do give back channel: Clare and Ravi were nodding, which told her the content was landing. A speaker who notices a still face can choose to read the room as a whole, keep to her plan, and, if it matters, check in words at the end, such as "Is there anything you'd like me to expand on?" Aisha now tells the people she trains to find the friendliest face in the room, present to them, and let the still faces be still.

She also learned to read note-taking as attention rather than judgment, and to find it reassuring rather than alarming.

Mr Grant, told later, began saying "thank you, that's helpful" after each answer.

moreCases.title: The husband who nodded too fast
moreCases.scene:
Leila and Sam have been married for six years. On a Sunday evening, Leila tries to tell Sam about something that has been worrying her
  for weeks: her mother's memory seems to be slipping, and she does not know whether to say anything to her brother. She speaks slowly, with
  pauses, working out what she thinks as she goes.

  Sam is listening, and wants to show it. He nods quickly and repeatedly, small fast nods, while she is still in the middle of her sentences,
  saying "yeah, yeah, yeah". When she pauses, he jumps in with what she should do: ring her brother tomorrow, book her mum a doctor's appointment.

  Leila goes quiet, says "Fine, I'll do that," and goes to run a bath. Sam is confused. He listened, he agreed, he helped. He asks her later what he
  did wrong, and she says that she felt hurried, as if he wanted her to finish.

Sam, for his part, had been brought up in a family where conversations were fast and everyone talked over each other. Fast nods and quick solutions were how love was shown in his house. Leila's family talked slowly, with long pauses, and nobody was rushed.

Leila's mother had been a teacher, and a precise, careful woman, and the first sign had been a lost purse and a forgotten appointment. Leila had been turning it over for a fortnight, unsure whether she was imagining it, and the conversation with Sam was the first time she had said any of it aloud.
moreCases.misread:
Sam read his fast nods as eager agreement and attention. Leila read the same nods as impatience, a signal to hurry up and get to the point, and his quick advice confirmed it.

Each of them was reading the other through their own family's conversational dialect, which is one of the most common and least noticed sources of misunderstanding between couples.

And his quick advice, meant to help, told her that he wanted the problem solved and the conversation finished, when what she wanted was to think aloud with someone beside her.
moreCases.betterRead:
Nods differ in speed, size and number, and the differences carry meaning. Rapid, small, repeated nods in the middle of someone's sentence often say "yes, yes, I've got it", which can mean move along or let me speak, however warmly they are meant. For someone working out a hard thought aloud, they feel like being hurried. Slow nods, at the end of phrases rather than in the middle, say "I hear you, go on," and leave room for the next pause. Sam's better approach, which he tried the following week, was to slow his nods to one at the end of each of Leila's sentences, to let the pauses be, and to ask a question rather than offer a plan: "What do you think your brother would say?" Leila talked for half an hour. At the end she decided, herself, to ring her brother, and thanked Sam for listening.

Sam also noticed, later, that his fast nods came most when he was anxious about the subject. Slowing them down meant sitting with his own discomfort, which was harder, and more useful, than offering a solution.

moreCases.title: The toss of the head that meant no
moreCases.scene:
Mark manages a small finance team in London. One of his analysts, Kostas, thirty-two, moved from Athens two years ago and is one of the
  most reliable people on the team. On a Thursday afternoon, Mark leans round Kostas's screen and asks whether the quarterly report will be ready
  for Friday's board meeting. Kostas, on the phone to a client, tilts his head back sharply, raises his eyebrows and makes a small click with his
  tongue. Mark takes it as a quick up-nod and goes back to his desk.

  On Friday morning, Mark asks for the report. Kostas looks surprised and says that he told Mark yesterday that it would not be ready until Monday,
  because the figures from the Manchester office had not arrived. Mark says that Kostas nodded. Kostas says that he did not nod at all.

  The board meeting starts at ten.

Kostas's English is fluent, and his colleagues rarely think of him as coming from anywhere else. That is part of why Mark did not think twice about the gesture: he heard Kostas as a Londoner, and read his head the same way.

The board meeting is the most important of the quarter. The chief executive has asked specifically for the report, and Mark had told her on Thursday evening, after the gesture, that it would be ready.
moreCases.misread:
Mark read Kostas's upward toss of the head as the casual up-nod he knew from London, a quick "yes". He did not consider that the same movement might carry a different meaning in Kostas's dialect.

And because Kostas was on the phone, he did not see Mark's reaction, and had no reason to think his answer had been misunderstood.

He also assumed that a gesture he did not fully recognise meant the thing he would most have liked it to mean. Wishful reading is a common partner of cross-cultural misreading, especially when a deadline is at stake.

Kostas's answer was perfectly clear in his own dialect, which is why he was surprised to be accused of nodding. From his side, he had said no.
moreCases.betterRead:
Head movements for yes and no are among the gestures people most often assume are universal, and they are not. In Greece, Cyprus and parts of Turkey, a quick upward toss of the head, often with raised eyebrows and a click of the tongue, commonly means no. To a London manager, it looks very like an up-nod. Kostas was answering clearly in his own dialect; Mark was reading it in his. The better practice, for anyone working across cultures, is to check important answers in words, especially when the answer is given by a gesture while someone is busy: "Is that a yes or a no?" It costs a second. Mark explained the delay to the board, who were understanding. Afterwards, he and Kostas laughed about it, and agreed that any answer about a deadline would be given in words. Kostas also admitted that, after two years in London, he sometimes did not know himself which dialect his head was speaking.

Mark also mentioned it, lightly, at the next team meeting, and two other colleagues admitted to similar confusions with gestures from home.

Kostas, in turn, now answers deadline questions with a word as well.

moreCases.title: The man who nodded at everything
moreCases.scene:
Mike, forty, is a quiet, well-liked engineer who hates conflict. In meetings, he nods along to almost everything: proposals, deadlines,
  criticism of his own team's work. At a planning meeting, the project lead sets an aggressive deadline for Mike's part of the project. Mike nods
  three times, slowly, as the date is announced, and says nothing. Inside, he is thinking that the date is impossible.

  Three weeks later, the deadline is missed. In the review, the project lead says, with some irritation, that Mike agreed to the date. Mike says
  that he did not agree to anything. The project lead points out that he nodded, in front of everyone.

  Mike goes home angry with the project lead, and then, slowly, with himself.

Mike's partner has noticed the same habit at home. He nods when she suggests holidays he does not want, plans he does not like and dinners with friends he finds dull, and then is quietly resentful for weeks.

Mike's team had told him before the meeting that the date was impossible, and he had promised them he would push back. When the date was announced and he nodded, two of his engineers looked at each other across the table and then down at their notepads. Afterwards, one of them asked him, quietly, what had happened, and Mike said he would sort it out. He never did.

In the review, the project lead also points out that the meeting notes, circulated the next day, recorded the date as agreed, and that Mike did not reply to say otherwise. Mike had read the notes and decided it was too late to object.
moreCases.misread:
The project lead read Mike's slow nods as agreement, which is what slow nods at a key moment usually seem to mean. Mike read his own nods as mere politeness, a way of showing that he had heard, and did not consider what they would look like from outside.

His silence after the nods compounded it. In a meeting, a nod followed by nothing is the clearest possible signal of agreement, whatever the nodder privately thinks.

The engineers' glance across the table, which Mike saw and ignored, was a back channel too: a silent signal that they had noticed the gap between what he had promised and what he had done.
moreCases.betterRead:
Nods are ambiguous: the same movement can mean I agree, I understand, I am listening or I am being polite. In a meeting, slow nods as a decision is announced will almost always be read as agreement, whatever the nodder means. Wells and Petty's research also suggests that nodding can nudge the nodder's own attitudes, and Briñol and Petty's that it increases confidence in whatever the nodder is already thinking; in Mike's case, it seems mainly to have shaped what others believed. The better habit is to use nods honestly, and to say what they cannot. If you do not agree, keep your head still and say so, or at least say that you have concerns: "I'm not sure that date works for my team. Can I come back to you by Friday?" Mike started doing that, haltingly at first. His team said it was the first time anyone had stood up for their workload, and the next deadline he agreed to, he met.

He also asked his partner to tell him when he nodded at home to something he did not want, which she found funny and did often.

workedReading.title: Reading the nods in a team meeting
workedReading.scene:
Grace manages a team of eight in a council housing department. She is presenting a plan to reorganise the team's caseloads, which will change who works with which tenants. As she speaks, she watches the room. Fatima nods slowly at the end of each point. Joe nods rapidly, small fast nods, from the start. Pete, who has been in the team longest, sits perfectly still, arms folded, with no nods at all. Lydia nods, but with a slight frown. Two others are nodding absently while glancing at their laptops.

Grace has presented changes to this team before, and she knows that people tend to nod in meetings and raise objections afterwards, in the corridor or by email. She would rather hear them now, while the plan can still change.

Grace has also had a long week, and she would like this meeting to go smoothly. She notices the wish, and reminds herself that a smooth meeting and a good decision are not the same thing.

The plan has taken her three months to prepare, and she has already discussed it with her own manager, who liked it. She is aware that the people in the room have had no say in it so far, and that the meeting is the first time they have seen it.

steps.label: Hear the back channel
steps.text:
Grace notices that the room is giving her a back channel, which tells her that people are following. She also notices that the nods are not all the same, and that she has been about to treat the room's nodding as general agreement. She reminds herself that nods mostly say "I'm listening", not "I agree".

She also notices her own reaction to the nods: relief. Relief is a sign that she wants agreement, which makes her more likely to see it where it is not.

She also notes that she has not yet heard a single word of response. Everything she has so far is body language, which is a lot of information about attention and very little about opinion.

steps.label: Read speed and timing
steps.text:
Fatima's slow nods at the end of each point fit someone taking it in and, perhaps, agreeing. Joe's rapid nods from the start look more like "yes, yes, I've got it": he may already know what he thinks, or want to speak. The absent nods from the two on their laptops are the easiest to discount. They are back channel on autopilot.

She also notices when the nods come. Fatima's come after Grace's explanations, not before them, which fits someone weighing each point rather than nodding in advance.

She also notices that Joe's fast nods began before she had explained the details, which suggests he made up his mind early, for or against, and that his view may not rest on the points she is making.

She also notes that Lydia's frown appears at a particular point, when Grace mentions the transfer of long-standing tenants. A change that is tied to a specific point is more informative than one that lasts the whole meeting.

steps.label: Check the baselines
steps.text:
Grace knows that Pete rarely nods in meetings, about anything, and that he folds his arms when he is concentrating. His stillness is his baseline, not necessarily disapproval. Lydia's frowning nod is less familiar: she usually nods with a smile. That change is the one Grace notes most.

She also reminds herself that Pete's stillness, in past meetings, has come before some of the most useful comments anyone made. A still face has often meant a man thinking hardest.

She also notes that one of the laptop nodders has stopped nodding and started typing, which may mean an email has arrived, or that something in the plan has prompted a note. She files it without deciding.

steps.label: Consider the rivals
steps.text:
Lydia's frown might mean disagreement, confusion about a detail, or worry about a particular tenant. Joe's fast nods might mean enthusiasm, impatience or a wish to raise something. Pete's stillness might mean concentration, scepticism or both. Grace notes that she cannot tell which from the nods, and that the decision about caseloads is too important to rest on them.

She also notes that the nods tell her about attention and mood, which is useful, and nothing reliable about agreement, which is what she most needs to know.

She also reminds herself that a room of nods is the norm in this organisation, where people rarely disagree in public. That culture makes the nods even less informative than usual.

steps.label: Ask in words
steps.text:
At the end of the presentation, Grace does not ask whether everyone is happy, which would invite more nods. She says, "I'd like to hear concerns as well as support. Lydia, you looked as though something was bothering you." Then, "Joe, you looked keen to say something." Then, to the room, "Pete, you know these tenants better than anyone. What am I missing?"

She names what she saw in neutral terms, "you looked as though something was bothering you", rather than "you don't like it". That leaves Lydia free to say what it was.

She keeps her own face open as she asks, and nods slowly as each person starts to answer. Her back channel now tells them that disagreement is welcome.

She also gives people a way to raise concerns privately, saying she will be in her office all afternoon, for anyone who would rather talk one to one.

steps.label: Hear what the nods hid
steps.text:
Lydia says that two of the tenants who would move to her caseload have had bad experiences with the officer they would be leaving, and that the change could upset them. Joe says he likes the plan and wants to start next week. Pete says, after a pause, that the plan is good but that the timing clashes with the annual rent review, and suggests waiting a month.

She also notices that Pete, once asked, speaks for longer than anyone. People who give little back channel often have the most to say when they are given a turn.

She also thanks each of them for the concern they raised, not just for the support. That small habit, repeated over months, makes it more likely that the next concern will be raised in the meeting rather than the corridor.

She also notes that none of the three concerns could have been read from a nod. Each came from knowledge the speaker had and Grace did not, which is the real reason for asking.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Grace adjusts the plan, moves the start date and arranges a careful handover for Lydia's two tenants. She notes that the room had nodded through her whole presentation, and that if she had taken the nods as agreement, she would have missed both of the problems that mattered most. She also notes that the still, unnodding man in the corner had the most useful thing to say.

She also changes how she runs similar meetings: she now ends every presentation by asking named people for concerns, and emails the plan afterwards with an invitation to reply privately.

She also follows up with the two laptop users afterwards, privately, to make sure they understood the change. Absent nods sometimes hide absent attention.

moreFailures.title: Treating a nod as a yes
moreFailures.body:
In ordinary conversation, a nod often seems to mean yes, and it is easy to carry that reading into meetings, negotiations and conversations across cultures, where it often means something else. Nods mostly say "I am listening" or "I follow". In some cultures, steady nodding is simply courteous attention, as Callum found in Osaka, and in others a movement that looks like a nod can mean no. Even within one office, a man may nod to be polite while disagreeing completely, as Mike did. When agreement matters, check it in words: "So we're agreed on Friday?" or "Is that a yes?" A nod is a reason to ask, not a contract.

It also helps to remember that nods in a group are contagious. When several people nod, others join in without thinking, and a room can look unanimous when only one or two people actually agree.

It also helps to watch for the opposite trap in negotiations, where a counterpart's steady nodding can create a feeling of progress that is not real. Summarise what you think has been agreed, aloud, and watch for hesitation.

Teachers and parents face a version of this every day. A child who nods when asked "Do you understand?" is often saying "I want this to be over". Asking the child to explain it back is a better test.

moreFailures.title: Reading a missing nod as disapproval
moreFailures.body:
A listener who gives no back channel is unnerving, and most speakers assume that silence means disapproval. Often it does not. Some people rarely nod by habit. Some concentrate with a still face. Senior people sometimes stay neutral deliberately, especially on interview panels. Some autistic people, and people from cultures with more restrained listening styles, nod less. On video calls, a missing nod may be a frozen screen. Before you change what you are saying to win a nod, look at the rest of the room, consider the rivals, and keep going. If it matters, ask afterwards.

It also helps to remember that people with depression, exhaustion or pain may give less back channel than usual. A listener who has gone still may be struggling, not judging.

Speakers who rely heavily on back channel can practise presenting to a still face, for example to a friend who agrees not to react, so that the real thing is less unsettling.

It also helps to give the still listener a role. Asking them a direct question early in a presentation, such as "Does this match what you've seen?", turns their silence into conversation.

And remember that your own stillness may be read the same way. If you are a listener who rarely nods, a word now and then, such as "go on" or "that's interesting", can save a speaker from falling apart.

moreFailures.title: Nodding when you do not agree
moreFailures.body:
Many people nod along out of politeness, conflict avoidance or a wish to show that they are listening, and then are surprised to find that others believed they agreed. In meetings especially, slow nods as a decision is announced will almost always be read as support. If you disagree, your nod is giving a false message, and silence after it is taken as consent. Keep your head still when you disagree, and say something, however small: "I've got some concerns about that," or "Can I think about it and come back to you?" Honest nods are part of honest speech.

It also helps to watch what happens to your own opinion when you nod along. Wells and Petty's research suggests that nodding can nudge your attitudes, so habitual nodding to things you doubt may slowly make them seem more acceptable than they are.

It also helps to know that disagreeing calmly in a meeting is almost always less costly than nodding and then missing a deadline. The awkward moment passes; the missed deadline is remembered.

In families, the same applies to children and teenagers who nod to end a conversation. A nod to "Will you be home by ten?" may mean "I heard you" rather than "I will".

moreFailures.title: Hurrying people with your nods
moreFailures.body:
Fast, repeated, small nods while someone is still speaking often feel to the speaker like being hurried, whatever the listener intends. They can say "I've got it, move on," or "I want to speak." For someone working out a hard thought, telling a painful story or choosing their words carefully, fast nods can close the conversation. When someone is struggling to say something, slow down: a single slow nod at the end of a phrase, a pause, a murmur. Let your nods follow their speech rather than run ahead of it.

It also helps to notice when you are nodding fast because you are impatient. Saying so, kindly, is often better than signalling it: "Sorry, I've got about five minutes. Can we come back to this tonight?"

It also helps to match the speaker's pace. A slow speaker needs slow nods; a fast, excited speaker may welcome quicker ones. Following their rhythm, rather than your own, is what makes a nod feel like listening.

It also helps to watch your nods when you are bored. Fast, absent nods while scrolling a phone are one of the clearest ways of telling someone you are not really listening, even if you are hearing every word.

questions.q: Are the up-nod and the down-nod real?
questions.a:
They are a folk taxonomy rather than a research finding. Many men in English-speaking countries describe the up-nod, a quick lift of the chin, as casual and familiar, and the down-nod, a short dip of the head, as more formal or respectful, and they use the two that way without ever having been taught. But the distinction has not been tested carefully, and it varies between places, generations and groups. Treat it as a useful local dialect rather than a rule. If you are new somewhere, watch how men nod at each other there before you assume that your own nods mean the same thing.

It also helps to notice your own default. Some men up-nod everyone, and some down-nod everyone. Neither is wrong, but each will land differently with different people.

It also helps to notice the nods men give each other in passing, on a street, at the gym or in a car park. They are among the easiest gestures to observe, and the dialects of a place show quickly once you start watching.

And in some places, men do not nod at strangers at all, and a nod from a stranger can seem forward. Like every greeting, the passing nod belongs to a place.

questions.q: Why do I nod even when I do not agree?
questions.a:
Because nodding does many jobs besides agreeing. Most nods in conversation are back channel, signals that you are listening and following, and they come almost automatically, which is why speakers falter without them. People also nod to be polite, to avoid conflict, to show respect for someone senior, or to keep a conversation moving. None of this is dishonest in itself. The problem arises when a nod is taken as agreement in a setting where agreement matters, such as a decision in a meeting. In those moments, notice your nod, and if it is giving the wrong message, say so in words.

It also helps to practise a neutral listening face for moments when you disagree: still, attentive, without nodding. It shows that you are listening without implying that you agree.

It also helps to notice whether your nods change with status. Many people nod more to senior colleagues than to junior ones, and some nod more to men than to women, without realising it.

You can also practise a small habit: when you nod, ask yourself, silently, whether you mean agreement or attention. After a few weeks, the difference becomes easier to feel.

questions.q: Can nodding make other people agree with me?
questions.a:
Not reliably, and this book does not teach it as a technique. Wells and Petty found that people who nodded while listening to an editorial agreed with it more than people who shook their heads, and Briñol and Petty later found that nodding seemed to increase people's confidence in their own thoughts: strong arguments became more persuasive, weak ones less so. These effects are about the nodder, and they are small. Trying to make someone nod in order to steer their opinion would be manipulation, and it is unlikely to work. Use your own nods honestly, to show attention and agreement where you mean them.

It also helps to remember that people notice when they are being worked on. Gestures used as techniques tend to look slightly off, and once someone suspects manipulation, they trust everything else you do less.

It also helps to remember that the research was done in laboratories, with editorials and headphones. Real conversations are messier, and small laboratory effects rarely translate into reliable everyday tools.

If you want to be more persuasive, the research points somewhere more useful: make stronger arguments, listen well, and let people reach their own conclusions.

questions.q: How should I nod on a video call?
questions.a:
A little more visibly than in person. On video, small nods are easily lost to low resolution, lag and the size of the window, so speakers get less back channel than they are used to, which is one reason video calls can feel tiring and flat. A slightly larger, slower nod at the end of a speaker's phrase, with your face clearly in frame, helps them know that you are following. Avoid nodding constantly, which looks odd on screen. The chapter on the video call body covers this in more detail.

It also helps to add a word or a small sound now and then, such as "right" or "mm", which travels better over video than a nod alone and gives the speaker a clearer back channel.

It also helps to look at the camera now and then while nodding, rather than at the speaker's image, so that your nod appears directed at them on their screen.

It also helps to keep your camera at eye level and your face well lit, so that the nods you do give are visible at all. A nod in a dark, low-angled frame is easily missed.

questions.q: What if someone never nods at all?
questions.a:
Then their stillness is probably their baseline, not a message. Some people nod very little by habit or temperament. In some cultures, listeners are more restrained. Some autistic people find nodding unnatural or tiring, and listen just as closely without it. Some people concentrate with a still face. If you are speaking to someone who never nods, watch for other signs of attention, such as eye contact, note-taking, questions or a turned body, and check understanding in words when it matters: "Does that make sense?" or "What do you think?"

It also helps to tell people about your own style if you rarely nod. "I don't nod much, but I'm listening" can save a speaker a lot of anxiety, especially in interviews and presentations.

It also helps to watch for small signs of attention that are not nods: a slight lean forward, a pen pausing, eyes moving to a slide. People who do not nod often show attention in these other ways.

And if you are a speaker who needs a nod to feel confident, it may help to know that most stillness is not judgment. The people who are thinking hardest about what you say are often the ones who move least.

questions.q: What does the Indian head wobble mean?
questions.a:
In many parts of South Asia, a side-to-side tilting of the head, often called the head wobble or head bobble, is a common way of signalling yes, okay, I understand or I am listening, and its meaning depends on speed, context and the person. To visitors, it can look like uncertainty or even a no, which leads to misunderstandings. The chapter on cultural variance in Part I describes a man who misread his mother-in-law's head tilt in exactly this way. As with any dialect, the best approach is to learn it from people who use it, to ask when you are unsure, and to check important answers in words.

It also helps to remember that people who use the head wobble may also be fluent in the international nod, and may switch between them depending on who they are talking to, which makes asking all the more useful.

It may also help to remember that people from any culture can find their own gestures misread abroad. Kostas's toss of the head and the head wobble are two examples among many; your own nod may be just as confusing somewhere else.

watch.title: The country where no means yes: Bulgaria
watch.notice: A short video on Bulgarian head movements for yes and no, which visitors often find reversed. Notice how confusing it is, and why confirming in words matters.

reviewPrompt: This week, notice every nod you give in one meeting and one conversation, and keep only the ones you mean.
